Reference: Farrokhi et al. (2025)

Model Setting

The paper studies deforestation in a dynamic world trading system: how trade barriers affect the extent, location and timing of forest loss. Four empirical patterns motivate the model (FAO data, 1990-2020): (1) global forest area fell by 7.1%, with about 90% of the loss in tropical countries and regrowth in Europe and China; (2) deforestation moves with agricultural land expansion; (3) countries with a revealed comparative advantage in agriculture in 1990 expanded agricultural land and lost more forest; (4) deforestation follows from a country's own population growth and that of its main trading partners. The model has a market for new land: a land-clearing sector uses labor to convert open-access forests into agricultural land, and forward-looking landowners buy new land and rent it to producers. Three mechanisms shape land use: (1) structural change determines the size of agriculture and the aggregate demand for land; (2) comparative advantage distributes the pressure on land across countries; (3) forward-looking land accumulation determines the timing of forest responses.

The paper first derives analytical results in a stylized steady state, then calibrates a quantitative version (40 countries/regions, multiple agricultural industries, manufacturing, services) and simulates the removal of agricultural tariffs, with and without UN population projections to 2100, including the carbon costs of deforestation.

Analytical Results

  • Proposition 1 (small open economy): a unilateral cut in iii's agricultural export costs raises its land stock (deforestation at home), governed by the import demand elasticity:

    dln⁡Lidln⁡di,A=Ni,MNi(1−η)<0for η>1(9.5.3.8)\frac{d\ln L_i}{d\ln d_{i,A}}=\frac{N_{i,M}}{N_i}(1-\eta)<0\quad\text{for }\eta>1 \tag{9.5.3.8}dlndi,A​dlnLi​​=Ni​Ni,M​​(1−η)<0for η>1(9.5.3.8)

    With tariffs instead of iceberg costs, (1−η)(1-\eta)(1−η) is replaced by (−η)(-\eta)(−η).

  • Proposition 2 (symmetric world): a global cut in agricultural trade costs lowers the global land stock when agriculture and manufacturing are complements, because the productivity gain from trade triggers structural change away from agriculture:

    dlog⁡Ldlog⁡dA=NMN(1−σ)(1−πAD)>0for σ<1(9.5.3.9)\frac{d\log L}{d\log d_A}=\frac{N_M}{N}(1-\sigma)\left(1-\pi_A^D\right)>0\quad\text{for }\sigma<1 \tag{9.5.3.9}dlogdA​dlogL​=NNM​​(1−σ)(1−πAD​)>0for σ<1(9.5.3.9)

    where πAD\pi_A^DπAD​ is the domestic expenditure share in agriculture. At the global scale the relevant elasticity is the sectoral one, 1−σ1-\sigma1−σ, not the import one, 1−η1-\eta1−η.

  • Proposition 3 (global tariffs): tariffs, unlike iceberg costs, do not carry an export-biased productivity gain. For a worldwide change in agricultural tariffs with symmetric countries:

    dln⁡Ldln⁡(1+tA)=NMN[(1−σ)(1−πAD)⏟(+) if σ<1+(η−1)(sAD−πAD)⏟(+) if η>1−(1−sAD)⏟(−)](9.5.3.10)\frac{d\ln L}{d\ln(1+t_A)}=\frac{N_M}{N}\Big[\underbrace{(1-\sigma)\left(1-\pi_A^D\right)}_{(+)\text{ if }\sigma<1}+\underbrace{(\eta-1)\left(s_A^D-\pi_A^D\right)}_{(+)\text{ if }\eta>1}\underbrace{-\left(1-s_A^D\right)}_{(-)}\Big] \tag{9.5.3.10}dln(1+tA​)dlnL​=NNM​​[(+) if σ<1(1−σ)(1−πAD​)​​+(+) if η>1(η−1)(sAD​−πAD​)​​(−)−(1−sAD​)​​](9.5.3.10)

    where sAD=πAD/(1−hA)s_A^D=\pi_A^D/(1-h_A)sAD​=πAD​/(1−hA​) is the share of farmers' revenue from domestic demand and hA=tA1+tA(1−πAD)h_A=\frac{t_A}{1+t_A}(1-\pi_A^D)hA​=1+tA​tA​​(1−πAD​) is the share of agricultural spending collected as tariffs. The last two terms capture changes in the pass-through of spending to farmers (and land). If η>σ\eta>\sigmaη>σ, land is U-shaped in tariffs: liberalization saves land if and only if initial tariffs exceed a critical rate tA∗t_A^*tA∗​:

    tA∗πAD(tA∗)=ση−σ,πAD(tA)=[(I−1)(dA(1+tA))1−η+1]−1(9.5.3.11)t_A^*\pi_A^D(t_A^*)=\frac{\sigma}{\eta-\sigma},\qquad \pi_A^D(t_A)=\left[(I-1)\left(d_A(1+t_A)\right)^{1-\eta}+1\right]^{-1} \tag{9.5.3.11}tA∗​πAD​(tA∗​)=η−σσ​,πAD​(tA​)=[(I−1)(dA​(1+tA​))1−η+1]−1(9.5.3.11)

  • Proposition 4 (comparative and absolute advantage): with a continuum of countries, homogeneous goods and Cobb-Douglas preferences (η→∞\eta\to\inftyη→∞, σ=1\sigma=1σ=1), moving from autarky to free trade makes countries specialize by comparative advantage Zi,A/Zi,MZ_{i,A}/Z_{i,M}Zi,A​/Zi,M​. If comparative and absolute advantage in agriculture are aligned (countries with high Zi,A/Zi,MZ_{i,A}/Z_{i,M}Zi,A​/Zi,M​ also have high Zi,AZ_{i,A}Zi,A​), free trade moves farming to the most efficient producers and global forest expands; otherwise it shrinks.

Together these extend Borlaug's hypothesis (productivity growth saves land when food demand is inelastic) to trade: trade acts like a technology improvement that can lower the global demand for land.

Calibration

  • Static block (circa 2010, GTAP 2014 trade, output and input-output data): σ=σI=0.5\sigma=\sigma^I=0.5σ=σI=0.5 (Comin et al. 2021), κ=κI=3\kappa=\kappa^I=3κ=κI=3 (Costinot et al. 2016), η=5\eta=5η=5 (Simonovska and Waugh 2014); αi,g,γi,g\alpha_{i,g},\gamma_{i,g}αi,g​,γi,g​ from GTAP and FAOSTAT; productivities Zi,gZ_{i,g}Zi,g​, demand shifters and trade costs from standard model inversion.

  • Tariffs: reported agricultural ad valorem tariffs are unreliable (specific tariffs, missing entries), so trade costs are split into τij,g=τij,g(non-policy)×τij,g(policy)\tau_{ij,g}=\tau_{ij,g}^{(non\text{-}policy)}\times\tau_{ij,g}^{(policy)}τij,g​=τij,g(non-policy)​×τij,g(policy)​, the policy part is estimated by a gravity regression on tariffs, FTAs and import fees, and its level is set with tariff revenue-to-import ratios (unweighted mean 13%).

  • Labor dynamics: 1/ν=21/\nu=21/ν=2, fNf^NfN equal to five times annual US income, ψ=1\psi=1ψ=1, ρ=0.05\rho=0.05ρ=0.05.

  • Land dynamics (novel block): regrowth rates δF=0.5%\delta_F=0.5\%δF​=0.5% and δO=5%\delta_O=5\%δO​=5% from Brazil's MapBiomas. In an inner loop, given {λ,γF,γO}\{\lambda,\gamma_F,\gamma_O\}{λ,γF​,γO​}, the shifters {ζi,F,ζi,O}\{\zeta_{i,F},\zeta_{i,O}\}{ζi,F​,ζi,O​} make the 2010 stocks of agricultural land, fallow land and forest a steady state. In an outer loop, by indirect inference, the model is shocked with UN population growth to 2100 and the elasticities minimize the distance between data and model coefficients from:

    log⁡(yi,t)−log⁡(yi,1990)=β0+βty[log⁡(Popi,2020)−log⁡(Popi,1990)]+ϵi,min⁡(β(data)−β(model))⊤(β(data)−β(model))(9.5.3.18)\log(y_{i,t})-\log(y_{i,1990})=\beta_0+\beta_t^y\left[\log(Pop_{i,2020})-\log(Pop_{i,1990})\right]+\epsilon_i,\qquad \min\left(\beta^{(data)}-\beta^{(model)}\right)^\top\left(\beta^{(data)}-\beta^{(model)}\right) \tag{9.5.3.18}log(yi,t​)−log(yi,1990​)=β0​+βty​[log(Popi,2020​)−log(Popi,1990​)]+ϵi​,min(β(data)−β(model))⊤(β(data)−β(model))(9.5.3.18)

Identification

  • γF\gamma_FγF​ vs. γO\gamma_OγO​: agricultural land expands partly from forest and partly from fallow land, so the separate responses of forest and agricultural area to population growth pin down the two labor elasticities.

  • λ\lambdaλ vs. γ\gammaγ: higher labor elasticities scale up the overall response, while a higher λ\lambdaλ lowers future clearing productivity and makes short-run responses relatively larger; the differences across 10-, 20- and 30-year horizons separate them.

  • ζi,F,ζi,O\zeta_{i,F},\zeta_{i,O}ζi,F​,ζi,O​: from initial land stocks being a steady state; ζi,F\zeta_{i,F}ζi,F​ correlates with measures of forest protection.

  • Validation: the fallow block is needed to match the land response to population; the model reproduces the (untargeted) effect of trading partners' population growth and correlates with observed yields.

Counterfactuals

  • Scenario 1: remove all tariffs on Brazilian agricultural exports (an 8.6 p.p. tariff cut). Brazil's forest share falls by 1 p.p. after 14 years, 2 p.p. after 42 years and 2.5 p.p. in the steady state; global forest area falls. Steady-state forest leakage (forest gain abroad per unit of forest lost in Brazil) is about 50%, and is larger in the short run because Brazil cannot reallocate workers to land clearing immediately.

  • Scenario 2: remove all agricultural tariffs globally. Global forest area rises by about 0.2 p.p. (12 million ha after 30 years, 20 million ha in the steady state), versus 291 million ha lost in 1990-2020. Structural change dominates the direct effect of lower tariffs. Behind the small aggregate change is large reallocation: Brazil, the US, Canada and Australia account for over three-quarters of the forest loss (1-3% of their forests), while forest expands in most tropical countries (e.g. Central Africa, Southeast Asia).

  • Mechanisms: with σ∈{1.5,3.0}\sigma\in\{1.5,3.0\}σ∈{1.5,3.0} (substitutes) Scenario 2 instead causes global forest loss, while Scenario 1 is qualitatively unchanged. Across countries, a stronger comparative advantage in agriculture predicts more forest loss (slope −0.777-0.777−0.777). Comparative and absolute advantage in agriculture are positively correlated, so global agricultural land falls by about 1% while land-weighted agricultural productivity rises by 8%, in line with Proposition 4.

  • Population growth (UN projections, 35% on average, over 300% in parts of Africa): large deforestation in Africa in the new baseline; global tariff removal then has a slightly negative effect on global forest, but shifts deforestation away from carbon-dense African forests.

  • Welfare: climate-adjusted welfare is C−ϕZC-\phi ZC−ϕZ (world real consumption minus the value of deforestation emissions, no sequestration from regrowth, 5% discount rate). Global tariff removal raises real consumption by 0.131%; with SCC = $200/tCO2_22​ the climate cost is 8.8% of 2010 US GDP and the net gain falls to 0.086% (about 30% of the gain eroded); with SCC = $350 it is 0.053%; with population growth the climate cost falls to 4.5% and the net gain is 0.159%. The net gain turns negative only if the SCC exceeds about $1,150. Brazil-only liberalization lowers global welfare (−0.090%-0.090\%−0.090% before climate costs). With σ=1.5\sigma=1.5σ=1.5 the model would wrongly predict climate costs of 37.5% of US GDP. Gains across countries rise with the deforestation the policy induces.

Extensions

  • Non-homothetic preferences (Comin et al. 2021) change little.

  • A tenfold increase in tariffs worldwide yields net welfare losses under all carbon-cost and population scenarios.

  • 30% sequestration from regrowth lowers climate costs. Without carbon heterogeneity across forests, about 55% sequestration would make climate costs zero; with heterogeneity, near-complete sequestration is needed, because relocation offsets the gain in area.

  • Dynamics matter: the first 5 years account for one-tenth of the present value of climate costs from global tariff removal, and the first 20 years for 78%.

  • Higher λ\lambdaλ for boreal and temperate countries reduces deforestation in Canada, the US and Australia but also limits regrowth elsewhere, leaving aggregates unchanged.

These are the three technologies of the stylized model, chosen to be as simple as possible so that the propositions have closed forms. Qi,AQ_{i,A}Qi,A​ is agricultural output, produced with cleared land LiL_iLi​ only, at a constant yield Zi,AZ_{i,A}Zi,A​ (output per unit of land). Qi,MQ_{i,M}Qi,M​ is manufacturing output, produced with labor Ni,MN_{i,M}Ni,M​ only, at labor productivity Zi,MZ_{i,M}Zi,M​. Qi,TQ_{i,T}Qi,T​ is the flow of new land cleared from forest per unit of time, produced with labor Ni,TN_{i,T}Ni,T​ only, at productivity Zi,TZ_{i,T}Zi,T​ (area cleared per worker per unit of time). Since agriculture uses no labor, the labor resource constraint is Ni=Ni,M+Ni,TN_i=N_{i,M}+N_{i,T}Ni​=Ni,M​+Ni,T​.

All three are linear, so unit costs do not depend on scale and prices are pinned down by factor prices alone, as in equation (3). The key feature is that land is not an endowment but a produced, depreciating asset: labor is turned into new land through the TTT sector, the stock then follows equation (5), and in the steady state Li=Zi,TNi,T/δLL_i=Z_{i,T}N_{i,T}/\delta_LLi​=Zi,T​Ni,T​/δL​ (equation (7)). The choice between manufacturing and land clearing is therefore the choice between producing manufactures and producing, indirectly, food. The linear clearing technology rules out rising marginal costs of deforestation as forest becomes scarce; the quantitative model restores them with the function Ji(zi)J_i(z_i)Ji​(zi​) and decreasing returns to labor in equation (14). The assumption that agriculture uses no labor and manufacturing no land is relaxed in equation (13).

The price of new land is the present value of future rents, discounted at the rate of time preference plus the regrowth hazard. This is the forward-looking element of the model: expected future agricultural demand raises qiq_iqi​ today and triggers clearing before rents actually rise. With constant rents the integral equals ri/(ρ+δL)r_i/(\rho+\delta_L)ri​/(ρ+δL​), the steady-state relation used in equation (7). The no-bubble condition and an active clearing sector are implicit in the note.

This is the law of motion of the stock of agricultural (cleared) land in the stylized model. L˙i\dot{L}_iL˙i​ is the change in the stock per unit of time; Qi,T=Zi,TNi,TQ_{i,T}=Z_{i,T}N_{i,T}Qi,T​=Zi,T​Ni,T​ is the gross flow of forest converted into farmland, from equation (2); and δLLi\delta_LL_iδL​Li​ is the area that reverts to forest, with δL>0\delta_L>0δL​>0 a constant regrowth rate. It has the same form as capital accumulation, K˙=I−δK\dot{K}=I-\delta KK˙=I−δK: clearing is investment and regrowth is depreciation.

Because the total area is fixed, Hi=Li+FiH_i=L_i+F_iHi​=Li​+Fi​, forest moves one-for-one in the opposite direction,

F˙i=−L˙i=δLLi−Zi,TNi,T\dot{F}_i=-\dot{L}_i=\delta_LL_i-Z_{i,T}N_{i,T}F˙i​=−L˙i​=δL​Li​−Zi,T​Ni,T​

First, land is a slow-moving state variable: for a constant clearing flow the stock converges to Qi,T/δLQ_{i,T}/\delta_LQi,T​/δL​ at rate δL\delta_LδL​, which is why policy responses take decades in the simulations. Second, keeping a positive stock requires a permanent flow of labor into clearing, so in the steady state land is effectively produced with labor, Li=Zi,TNi,T/δLL_i=Z_{i,T}N_{i,T}/\delta_LLi​=Zi,T​Ni,T​/δL​ (equation (7)); this is what links the land stock to the allocation of labor in Propositions 1 to 3. The specification abstracts from fallow land, so that L˙i=−F˙i\dot{L}_i=-\dot{F}_iL˙i​=−F˙i​ always holds; the quantitative model breaks this link in equation (16).

The form buys two sources of rising marginal cost that the linear technology of equation (2) lacks. Within a period, γF<1\gamma_F<1γF​<1 means decreasing returns to clearing labor, so a larger clearing flow has a higher marginal cost; this bounds the speed of adjustment. Hence 1/ν1/\nu1/ν is the elasticity of sectoral labor flows to value differences: as ν→0\nu\to0ν→0 workers go to the best sector with certainty, and as ν→∞\nu\to\inftyν→∞ moves are random. Sectoral employment then evolves as N˙i,s′=ψ(∑sμi,ss′Ni,s−Ni,s′)\dot{N}_{i,s'}=\psi\left(\sum_s\mu_{i,ss'}N_{i,s}-N_{i,s'}\right)N˙i,s′​=ψ(∑s​μi,ss′​Ni,s​−Ni,s′​). These frictions slow the flow of workers into land clearing, which is why forest responses, and leakage, differ between the short and the long run. The closed form for Wi,sW_{i,s}Wi,s​ without an additive constant νγˉ\nu\bar{\gamma}νγˉ​ relies on the mean-zero normalization of the shocks, which the note does not state; with standard (non-centered) shocks a constant would appear, without affecting the move probabilities.

The equation has two parts: an auxiliary cross-country regression and the indirect-inference criterion built on it. In the regression, iii indexes countries, yi,ty_{i,t}yi,t​ is either forest area or agricultural land area in year t∈{2000,2010,2020}t\in\{2000,2010,2020\}t∈{2000,2010,2020}, and the left-hand side is its log change since 1990, over horizons of 10, 20 and 30 years. The regressor is the log growth of population between 1990 and 2020, the same for all horizons. βty\beta_t^yβty​ is thus the elasticity of the change in land type yyy at horizon ttt with respect to 30-year population growth, β0\beta_0β0​ is a constant and ϵi\epsilon_iϵi​ an error. With two outcomes and three horizons there are six coefficients, stacked in the vector β\betaβ.

The coefficients are not given a causal interpretation; they are descriptive moments. The same regressions are run on data simulated from the model, in which the 2010 steady state is shocked with the path of population, and the three parameters (λ,γF,γO)(\lambda,\gamma_F,\gamma_O)(λ,γF​,γO​) of equation (14) are chosen to solve

(λ^,γ^F,γ^O)=arg⁡min⁡λ,γF,γO(β(data)−β(model)(λ,γF,γO))⊤(β(data)−β(model)(λ,γF,γO))\left(\hat{\lambda},\hat{\gamma}_F,\hat{\gamma}_O\right)=\arg\min_{\lambda,\gamma_F,\gamma_O}\left(\beta^{(data)}-\beta^{(model)}(\lambda,\gamma_F,\gamma_O)\right)^\top\left(\beta^{(data)}-\beta^{(model)}(\lambda,\gamma_F,\gamma_O)\right)(λ^,γ^​F​,γ^​O​)=argλ,γF​,γO​min​(β(data)−β(model)(λ,γF​,γO​))⊤(β(data)−β(model)(λ,γF​,γO​))

with identity weighting; for every candidate, the shifters ζi,F,ζi,O\zeta_{i,F},\zeta_{i,O}ζi,F​,ζi,O​ are reset so that the 2010 stocks are a steady state of equation (16). There are six moments for three parameters, so the system is over-identified. Identification is intuitive: population growth raises food demand and land prices; γF\gamma_FγF​ and γO\gamma_OγO​ govern how elastically clearing from forest and from fallow land respond (equation (15)), so the forest and farmland coefficients separate them; and λ\lambdaλ governs how fast clearing productivity falls as the stock is used up, so it is pinned down by how the coefficients change between the 10-, 20- and 30-year horizons. The estimates are λ=0.9\lambda=0.9λ=0.9, γF=0.95\gamma_F=0.95γF​=0.95 and γO=0.9\gamma_O=0.9γO​=0.9.
